### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.
While TDP-43 has been primarily studied in neurodegenerative diseases [ 17 , 18 ], emerging evidence underscores its role as a multifaceted RNA-binding protein that drives cancer progression through diverse post-transcriptional mechanisms. TDP-43 regulates gene expression by modulating alternative splicing, mRNA stability, miRNA biogenesis, and lncRNA interactions [ 10 ]. For example, in triple-negative breast

### The HIF1-TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells
After confirming the regulatory link between HIF-1α and TDP-43, we sought to evaluate the functional necessity of this axis in mediating hypoxia-driven cancer progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis. To functionally characterize the HIF1- TARDBP axis, we first established efficient TARDBP knockdown and HIF1A overexpression models in SW480 and HCT116 cells, as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting ( Fig. 3 A-D). Under hypoxic conditions, TARDBP depletion significantly attenuated hypoxia-induced cell proliferation, migration, and invasion ( Fig. 3 E-G). Crucially, these suppressive effects were markedly rescued by ectopic expression of HIF1A ( Fig. 3 E-G), indicating that HIF1 functions upstream of TDP-43 to drive these malignant behaviors.

### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.
While TDP-43 has been primarily studied in neurodegenerative diseases [ 17 , 18 ], emerging evidence underscores its role as a multifaceted RNA-binding protein that drives cancer progression through diverse post-transcriptional mechanisms. TDP-43 regulates gene expression by modulating alternative splicing, mRNA stability, miRNA biogenesis, and lncRNA interactions [ 10 ]. For example, in triple-negative breast

### Highlights
• Hypoxia induces TDP-43 via HIF-1α binding to HRE3 in its promoter.
• TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA through RRM domain-mediated interaction.
• TARDBP knockdown suppresses CRC metastasis and angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo .
• TRIP6 rescues malignant phenotypes inhibited by TARDBP silencing.

### Graphical abstract
Under hypoxia, HIF1 binds to the HRE3 site and transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP . TDP-43, via its RRM1 and RRM2 domains, stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to enhance its expression, ultimately driving CRC cell migration, invasion, and angiogenesis.

### Introduction
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with tumor metastasis being the primary cause of treatment failure and poor prognosis [ 1 ]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in driving cancer progression, and hypoxia is a key hallmark of advanced solid tumors [ 2 ]. Rapidly proliferating cancer cells outstrip the oxygen supply from existing vasculature, creating hypoxic regions that activate adaptive signaling pathways [ 3 ]. Clinically, tumor hypoxia has been directly linked to more aggressive phenotypes and poor patient outcomes. For instance, studies using 18F-fluoromisonidazole (FMISO) PET imaging have demonstrated that significant hypoxia is a robust indicator of increased distant metastasis risk and higher rates of disease progression [ 4 , 5 ]. Furthermore, hypoxia has been identified as an independent predictor of poor overall survival (OS) in various clinical cohorts [ 6 ]. The master regulator of cellular response to hypoxia, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), orchestrates the expression of numerous genes promoting angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and invasion [ 7 ]. Notably, tumor angiogenesis, stimulated by hypoxia-induced factors like VEGF, is essential for supplying nutrients and oxygen, thereby facilitating tumor growth and metastatic spread. Despite the established role of hypoxia in CRC aggressiveness, the complete repertoire of downstream effectors and the intricate molecular networks linking hypoxia to CRC metastasis remain incompletely elucidated.
TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), encoded by the TARDBP gene, is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein predominantly known for its role in neurodegenerative diseases [ 8 , 9 ]. However, emerging evidence suggests an oncogenic function for TDP-43 in various cancers, where it regulates gene expression at multiple levels, including mRNA stability and alternative splicing [ 10 ]. TDP-43 contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM

### Bioinformatic analysis
The mRNA expression data of TARDBP (encoding TDP-43) and HIF1A in CRC and adjacent normal tissues were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ). The protein expression level of TDP-43 in colon cancer was analyzed using data from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) via the UALCAN portal ( http://ualcan.path.uab.edu ). The correlation between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in TCGA CRC samples was evaluated using Pearson’s correlation analysis.

### Animal housing
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Second Clinical College of Zhengzhou University and conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Female BALB/c nude mice (6 weeks old) were purchased from Beijing Huafukang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle, controlled temperature (22±2°C), and humidity (50±10%). Food and water were provided ad libitum. All efforts were made to minimize animal suffering.

### Results
TARDBP is upregulated in CRC and correlates with HIF1A expression
We first evaluated the clinical significance of TDP-43 in CRC by analyzing public datasets to determine whether its expression is altered in tumor tissues and associated with hypoxia-related signaling. Analysis of TCGA RNA-seq data revealed that TARDBP mRNA levels were significantly elevated in CRC tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues ( Fig. 1 A). Consistent with this finding, protein expression data from the CPTAC confirmed a significant increase in TDP-43 protein levels in colon tumors ( Fig. 1 B). Given the central role of hypoxia and its master regulator HIF-1α in cancer progression, we further examined their relationship. Notably, correlation analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in CRC cohorts (Pearson R =0.277, P &lt; 0.001) ( Fig. 1 C). While this relatively weak correlation likely reflects the cellular heterogeneity and temporal dynamics inherent to bulk tumor transcriptomic data, it provided the initial clinical rationale to investigate a potential regulatory relationship between HIF1A and TARDBP . This hypothesis was subsequently validated through direct mechanistic experiments, as described below.

### Hypoxia induces TDP-43 expression through HIF1-dependent transcriptional regulation in CRC cells
Based on the positive clinical correlation observed between TARDBP and HIF1A , we hypothesized that TDP-43 expression is directly controlled by the master hypoxia regulator, HIF1, under hypoxic conditions. Under hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ), TARDBP mRNA and protein levels were significantly induced in a time-dependent manner in SW480 and HCT116 cells, paralleling the induction of HIF-1α protein ( Fig. 2 A, B). To investigate if this hypoxic induction is mediated by HIF1, we efficiently knocked down HIF1A using specific shRNAs ( Fig. 2 C, D). Notably, HIF1A depletion markedly attenuated the hypoxia-induced upregulation of TDP-43 protein ( Fig. 2 E), indicating that HIF1A is necessary for TDP-43 induction under hypoxia.

### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.
While TDP-43 has been primarily studied in neurodegenerative diseases [ 17 , 18 ], emerging evidence underscores its role as a multifaceted RNA-binding protein that drives cancer progression through diverse post-transcriptional mechanisms. ### Highlights
• Hypoxia induces TDP-43 via HIF-1α binding to HRE3 in its promoter.
• TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA through RRM domain-mediated interaction.
• TARDBP knockdown suppresses CRC metastasis and angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo .
• TRIP6 rescues malignant phenotypes inhibited by TARDBP silencing.

### Graphical abstract
Under hypoxia, HIF1 binds to the HRE3 site and transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP . TDP-43, via its RRM1 and RRM2 domains, stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to enhance its expression, ultimately driving CRC cell migration, invasion, and angiogenesis.

### Introduction
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with tumor metastasis being the primary cause of treatment failure and poor prognosis [ 1 ]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in driving cancer progression, and hypoxia is a key hallmark of advanced solid tumors [ 2 ]. Rapidly proliferating cancer cells outstrip the oxygen supply from existing vasculature, creating hypoxic regions that activate adaptive signaling pathways [ 3 ]. Clinically, tumor hypoxia has been directly linked to more aggressive phenotypes and poor patient outcomes. For instance, studies using 18F-fluoromisonidazole (FMISO) PET imaging have demonstrated that significant hypoxia is a robust indicator of increased distant metastasis risk and higher rates of disease progression [ 4 , 5 ]. Furthermore, hypoxia has been identified as an independent predictor of poor overall survival (OS) in various clinical cohorts [ 6 ]. The master regulator of cellular response to hypoxia, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), orchestrates the expression of numerous genes promoting angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and invasion [ 7 ]. Notably, tumor angiogenesis, stimulated by hypoxia-induced factors like VEGF, is essential for supplying nutrients and oxygen, thereby facilitating tumor growth and metastatic spread. Despite the established role of hypoxia in CRC aggressiveness, the complete repertoire of downstream effectors and the intricate molecular networks linking hypoxia to CRC metastasis remain incompletely elucidated.
TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), encoded by the TARDBP gene, is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein predominantly known for its role in neurodegenerative diseases [ 8 , 9 ]. However, emerging evidence suggests an oncogenic function for TDP-43 in various cancers, where it regulates gene expression at multiple levels, including mRNA stability and alternative splicing [ 10 ]. TDP-43 contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM

### Bioinformatic analysis
The mRNA expression data of TARDBP (encoding TDP-43) and HIF1A in CRC and adjacent normal tissues were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ). The protein expression level of TDP-43 in colon cancer was analyzed using data from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) via the UALCAN portal ( http://ualcan.path.uab.edu ). The correlation between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in TCGA CRC samples was evaluated using Pearson’s correlation analysis.

### Animal housing
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Second Clinical College of Zhengzhou University and conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Female BALB/c nude mice (6 weeks old) were purchased from Beijing Huafukang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle, controlled temperature (22±2°C), and humidity (50±10%). Food and water were provided ad libitum. All efforts were made to minimize animal suffering.

### Results
TARDBP is upregulated in CRC and correlates with HIF1A expression
We first evaluated the clinical significance of TDP-43 in CRC by analyzing public datasets to determine whether its expression is altered in tumor tissues and associated with hypoxia-related signaling. Analysis of TCGA RNA-seq data revealed that TARDBP mRNA levels were significantly elevated in CRC tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues ( Fig. 1 A). Consistent with this finding, protein expression data from the CPTAC confirmed a significant increase in TDP-43 protein levels in colon tumors ( Fig. 1 B). Given the central role of hypoxia and its master regulator HIF-1α in cancer progression, we further examined their relationship. Notably, correlation analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in CRC cohorts (Pearson R =0.277, P &lt; 0.001) ( Fig. 1 C). While this relatively weak correlation likely reflects the cellular heterogeneity and temporal dynamics inherent to bulk tumor transcriptomic data, it provided the initial clinical rationale to investigate a potential regulatory relationship between HIF1A and TARDBP . This hypothesis was subsequently validated through direct mechanistic experiments, as described below.

### Hypoxia induces TDP-43 expression through HIF1-dependent transcriptional regulation in CRC cells
Based on the positive clinical correlation observed between TARDBP and HIF1A , we hypothesized that TDP-43 expression is directly controlled by the master hypoxia regulator, HIF1, under hypoxic conditions. Under hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ), TARDBP mRNA and protein levels were significantly induced in a time-dependent manner in SW480 and HCT116 cells, paralleling the induction of HIF-1α protein ( Fig. 2 A, B). To investigate if this hypoxic induction is mediated by HIF1, we efficiently knocked down HIF1A using specific shRNAs ( Fig. 2 C, D). Notably, HIF1A depletion markedly attenuated the hypoxia-induced upregulation of TDP-43 protein ( Fig. 2 E), indicating that HIF1A is necessary for TDP-43 induction under hypoxia.

(A-B) SW480 and HCT116 cells were exposed to hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ) for the indicated times. (A) TARDBP mRNA levels were measured by RT-qPCR. Data are normalized to normoxic control (0 h). (B) Protein levels of TDP-43 and HIF-1α were analyzed by Western blotting. β-actin served as a loading control. (C-D) Validation of HIF1A knockdown efficiency in SW480 and HCT116 cells transfected with shRNA targeting HIF1A (sh HIF1A ) or non-targeting control (shNC). Efficiency was confirmed by (C) RT-qPCR and (D) Western blotting. (E) Western blot analysis of TDP-43 protein levels in SW480 and HCT116 cells transfected with shNC or sh HIF1A and then exposed to hypoxia (1% O 2 , 24 h). (F) Luciferase reporter assay in HEK293T cells co-transfected with a TARDBP promoter reporter construct and either HIF1A overexpression plasmid ( HIF1A ) or empty vector control (Vec). Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity. (G) Luciferase activity of serial 5’-truncation mutants of the TARDBP promoter co-transfected with HIF1A into HEK293T cells. The location of putative hypoxia-response elements (HREs) is indicated. (H) ChIP assays w

### The HIF1-TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells
After confirming the regulatory link between HIF-1α and TDP-43, we sought to evaluate the functional necessity of this axis in mediating hypoxia-driven cancer progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis. To functionally characterize the HIF1- TARDBP axis, we first established efficient TARDBP knockdown and HIF1A overexpression models in SW480 and HCT116 cells, as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting ( Fig. 3 A-D). Under hypoxic conditions, TARDBP depletion significantly attenuated hypoxia-induced cell proliferation, migration, and invasion ( Fig. 3 E-G). Crucially, these suppressive effects were markedly rescued by ectopic expression of HIF1A ( Fig. 3 E-G), indicating that HIF1 functions upstream of TDP-43 to drive these malignant behaviors.
The HIF1- TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells. (A-D) Validation of gene manipulation efficiency. Knockdown and overexpression efficiency were confirmed by (A, C) qRT-PCR and (B, D) Western blotting. (E-I) Functional assays were performed in cells subjected to the following treatments: Normoxia, Hypoxia, Hypoxia+shNC, Hypoxia+sh TARDBP , Hypoxia+sh TARDBP +Vec, Hypoxia+sh TARDBP + HIF1A . (E) Cell proliferation was assessed by CCK-8 assay. (F) Cell migration was evaluated by Transwell assay (without Matrigel coating). Representative images (left) and quantitative analysis (right) are shown. (G) Cell invasion was evaluated by Transwell assay (with Matrigel coating). Representative images (left) and quantitative analysis (right) are shown. (H) Angiogenesis was assessed using the CAM assay. ### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.
While TDP-43 has been primarily studied in neurodegenerative diseases [ 17 , 18 ], emerging evidence underscores its role as a multifaceted RNA-binding protein that drives cancer progression through diverse post-transcriptional mechanisms. TDP-43 regulates gene expression by modulating alternative splicing, mRNA stability, miRNA biogenesis, and lncRNA interactions [ 10 ]. For example, in triple-negative breast

Transl Oncol . 2026 Jun 12;70:102817. doi: 10.1016/j.tranon.2026.102817
HIF1-driven TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to drive angiogenesis and colorectal cancer progression under hypoxia

### Ke Cheng
a The Second Clinical College of Zhengzhou University, No. 127, Dongming Road, Jinshui District, Zhengzhou 450003, China

### Yonggang Liu
b The Affiliated Cancer Hospital of Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou 450003, China

⁎ Corresponding author. binhao688@126.com
Received 2025 Dec 11; Revised 2026 Apr 2; Accepted 2026 May 11; Collection date 2026 Aug.
This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/).
PMCID: PMC13279019 PMID: 42284709

### Highlights
• Hypoxia induces TDP-43 via HIF-1α binding to HRE3 in its promoter.
• TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA through RRM domain-mediated interaction.
• TARDBP knockdown suppresses CRC metastasis and angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo .
• TRIP6 rescues malignant phenotypes inhibited by TARDBP silencing.

### Graphical abstract
Under hypoxia, HIF1 binds to the HRE3 site and transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP . TDP-43, via its RRM1 and RRM2 domains, stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to enhance its expression, ultimately driving CRC cell migration, invasion, and angiogenesis.

### Introduction
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with tumor metastasis being the primary cause of treatment failure and poor prognosis [ 1 ]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in driving cancer progression, and hypoxia is a key hallmark of advanced solid tumors [ 2 ]. Rapidly proliferating cancer cells outstrip the oxygen supply from existing vasculature, creating hypoxic regions that activate adaptive signaling pathways [ 3 ]. Clinically, tumor hypoxia has been directly linked to more aggressive phenotypes and poor patient outcomes. For instance, studies using 18F-fluoromisonidazole (FMISO) PET imaging have demonstrated that significant hypoxia is a robust indicator of increased distant metastasis risk and higher rates of disease progression [ 4 , 5 ]. Furthermore, hypoxia has been identified as an independent predictor of poor overall survival (OS) in various clinical cohorts [ 6 ]. The master regulator of cellular response to hypoxia, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), orchestrates the expression of numerous genes promoting angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and invasion [ 7 ]. Notably, tumor angiogenesis, stimulated by hypoxia-induced factors like VEGF, is essential for supplying nutrients and oxygen, thereby facilitating tumor growth and metastatic spread. Despite the established role of hypoxia in CRC aggressiveness, the complete repertoire of downstream effectors and the intricate molecular networks linking hypoxia to CRC metastasis remain incompletely elucidated.
TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), encoded by the TARDBP gene, is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein predominantly known for its role in neurodegenerative diseases [ 8 , 9 ]. However, emerging evidence suggests an oncogenic function for TDP-43 in various cancers, where it regulates gene expression at multiple levels, including mRNA stability and alternative splicing [ 10 ]. TDP-43 contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM

### Bioinformatic analysis
The mRNA expression data of TARDBP (encoding TDP-43) and HIF1A in CRC and adjacent normal tissues were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ). The protein expression level of TDP-43 in colon cancer was analyzed using data from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) via the UALCAN portal ( http://ualcan.path.uab.edu ). The correlation between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in TCGA CRC samples was evaluated using Pearson’s correlation analysis.

### Animal housing
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Second Clinical College of Zhengzhou University and conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Female BALB/c nude mice (6 weeks old) were purchased from Beijing Huafukang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle, controlled temperature (22±2°C), and humidity (50±10%). Food and water were provided ad libitum. All efforts were made to minimize animal suffering.

### Results
TARDBP is upregulated in CRC and correlates with HIF1A expression
We first evaluated the clinical significance of TDP-43 in CRC by analyzing public datasets to determine whether its expression is altered in tumor tissues and associated with hypoxia-related signaling. Analysis of TCGA RNA-seq data revealed that TARDBP mRNA levels were significantly elevated in CRC tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues ( Fig. 1 A). Consistent with this finding, protein expression data from the CPTAC confirmed a significant increase in TDP-43 protein levels in colon tumors ( Fig. 1 B). Given the central role of hypoxia and its master regulator HIF-1α in cancer progression, we further examined their relationship. Notably, correlation analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in CRC cohorts (Pearson R =0.277, P &lt; 0.001) ( Fig. 1 C). While this relatively weak correlation likely reflects the cellular heterogeneity and temporal dynamics inherent to bulk tumor transcriptomic data, it provided the initial clinical rationale to investigate a potential regulatory relationship between HIF1A and TARDBP . This hypothesis was subsequently validated through direct mechanistic experiments, as described below.

### Hypoxia induces TDP-43 expression through HIF1-dependent transcriptional regulation in CRC cells
Based on the positive clinical correlation observed between TARDBP and HIF1A , we hypothesized that TDP-43 expression is directly controlled by the master hypoxia regulator, HIF1, under hypoxic conditions. Under hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ), TARDBP mRNA and protein levels were significantly induced in a time-dependent manner in SW480 and HCT116 cells, paralleling the induction of HIF-1α protein ( Fig. 2 A, B). To investigate if this hypoxic induction is mediated by HIF1, we efficiently knocked down HIF1A using specific shRNAs ( Fig. 2 C, D). Notably, HIF1A depletion markedly attenuated the hypoxia-induced upregulation of TDP-43 protein ( Fig. 2 E), indicating that HIF1A is necessary for TDP-43 induction under hypoxia.

(A-B) SW480 and HCT116 cells were exposed to hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ) for the indicated times. (A) TARDBP mRNA levels were measured by RT-qPCR. Data are normalized to normoxic control (0 h). (B) Protein levels of TDP-43 and HIF-1α were analyzed by Western blotting. β-actin served as a loading control. (C-D) Validation of HIF1A knockdown efficiency in SW480 and HCT116 cells transfected with shRNA targeting HIF1A (sh HIF1A ) or non-targeting control (shNC). Efficiency was confirmed by (C) RT-qPCR and (D) Western blotting. (E) Western blot analysis of TDP-43 protein levels in SW480 and HCT116 cells transfected with shNC or sh HIF1A and then exposed to hypoxia (1% O 2 , 24 h). (F) Luciferase reporter assay in HEK293T cells co-transfected with a TARDBP promoter reporter construct and either HIF1A overexpression plasmid ( HIF1A ) or empty vector control (Vec). Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity. (G) Luciferase activity of serial 5’-truncation mutants of the TARDBP promoter co-transfected with HIF1A into HEK293T cells. The location of putative hypoxia-response elements (HREs) is indicated. (H) ChIP assays w

### The HIF1-TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells
After confirming the regulatory link between HIF-1α and TDP-43, we sought to evaluate the functional necessity of this axis in mediating hypoxia-driven cancer progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis. To functionally characterize the HIF1- TARDBP axis, we first established efficient TARDBP knockdown and HIF1A overexpression models in SW480 and HCT116 cells, as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting ( Fig. 3 A-D). Under hypoxic conditions, TARDBP depletion significantly attenuated hypoxia-induced cell proliferation, migration, and invasion ( Fig. 3 E-G). Crucially, these suppressive effects were markedly rescued by ectopic expression of HIF1A ( Fig. 3 E-G), indicating that HIF1 functions upstream of TDP-43 to drive these malignant behaviors.
The HIF1- TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells. (A-D) Validation of gene manipulation efficiency. SW480 and HCT116 cells were transfected with shRNA targeting TARDBP (sh TARDBP ) or non-targeting control (shNC) (A, B), or with a HIF1A overexpression plasmid ( HIF1A ) or empty vector control (Vec) (C, D). Knockdown and overexpression efficiency were confirmed by (A, C) qRT-PCR and (B, D) Western blotting. (E-I) Functional assays were performed in cells subjected to the following treatments: Normoxia, Hypoxia, Hypoxia+shNC, Hypoxia+sh TARDBP , Hypoxia+sh TARDBP +Vec, Hypoxia+sh TARDBP + HIF1A . (E) Cell proliferation was assessed by CCK-8 assay. (F) Cell migration was evaluated by Transwell assay (without Matrigel coating). Representative images (left) and quantitative analysis (right) are shown. (G) Cell invasion was evaluated by Transwell assay (with Matrigel coating). Representative images (left) and quantitative analysis (right) are shown. (H) Angiogenesis was assessed using the CAM assay. ### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.
While TDP-43 has been primarily studied in neurodegenerative diseases [ 17 , 18 ], emerging evidence underscores its role as a multifaceted RNA-binding protein that drives cancer progression through diverse post-transcriptional mechanisms. TDP-43 regulates gene expression by modulating alternative splicing, mRNA stability, miRNA biogenesis, and lncRNA interactions [ 10 ]. For example, in triple-negative breast

### Highlights
• Hypoxia induces TDP-43 via HIF-1α binding to HRE3 in its promoter.
• TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA through RRM domain-mediated interaction.
• TARDBP knockdown suppresses CRC metastasis and angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo .
• TRIP6 rescues malignant phenotypes inhibited by TARDBP silencing.

### Graphical abstract
Under hypoxia, HIF1 binds to the HRE3 site and transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP . TDP-43, via its RRM1 and RRM2 domains, stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to enhance its expression, ultimately driving CRC cell migration, invasion, and angiogenesis.

### Introduction
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with tumor metastasis being the primary cause of treatment failure and poor prognosis [ 1 ]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in driving cancer progression, and hypoxia is a key hallmark of advanced solid tumors [ 2 ]. Rapidly proliferating cancer cells outstrip the oxygen supply from existing vasculature, creating hypoxic regions that activate adaptive signaling pathways [ 3 ]. Clinically, tumor hypoxia has been directly linked to more aggressive phenotypes and poor patient outcomes. For instance, studies using 18F-fluoromisonidazole (FMISO) PET imaging have demonstrated that significant hypoxia is a robust indicator of increased distant metastasis risk and higher rates of disease progression [ 4 , 5 ]. Furthermore, hypoxia has been identified as an independent predictor of poor overall survival (OS) in various clinical cohorts [ 6 ]. The master regulator of cellular response to hypoxia, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), orchestrates the expression of numerous genes promoting angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and invasion [ 7 ]. Notably, tumor angiogenesis, stimulated by hypoxia-induced factors like VEGF, is essential for supplying nutrients and oxygen, thereby facilitating tumor growth and metastatic spread. Despite the established role of hypoxia in CRC aggressiveness, the complete repertoire of downstream effectors and the intricate molecular networks linking hypoxia to CRC metastasis remain incompletely elucidated.
TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), encoded by the TARDBP gene, is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein predominantly known for its role in neurodegenerative diseases [ 8 , 9 ]. However, emerging evidence suggests an oncogenic function for TDP-43 in various cancers, where it regulates gene expression at multiple levels, including mRNA stability and alternative splicing [ 10 ]. TDP-43 contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM

### Bioinformatic analysis
The mRNA expression data of TARDBP (encoding TDP-43) and HIF1A in CRC and adjacent normal tissues were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ). The protein expression level of TDP-43 in colon cancer was analyzed using data from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) via the UALCAN portal ( http://ualcan.path.uab.edu ). The correlation between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in TCGA CRC samples was evaluated using Pearson’s correlation analysis.

### Animal housing
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Second Clinical College of Zhengzhou University and conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Female BALB/c nude mice (6 weeks old) were purchased from Beijing Huafukang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle, controlled temperature (22±2°C), and humidity (50±10%). Food and water were provided ad libitum. All efforts were made to minimize animal suffering.

### Results
TARDBP is upregulated in CRC and correlates with HIF1A expression
We first evaluated the clinical significance of TDP-43 in CRC by analyzing public datasets to determine whether its expression is altered in tumor tissues and associated with hypoxia-related signaling. Analysis of TCGA RNA-seq data revealed that TARDBP mRNA levels were significantly elevated in CRC tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues ( Fig. 1 A). Consistent with this finding, protein expression data from the CPTAC confirmed a significant increase in TDP-43 protein levels in colon tumors ( Fig. 1 B). Given the central role of hypoxia and its master regulator HIF-1α in cancer progression, we further examined their relationship. Notably, correlation analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in CRC cohorts (Pearson R =0.277, P &lt; 0.001) ( Fig. 1 C). While this relatively weak correlation likely reflects the cellular heterogeneity and temporal dynamics inherent to bulk tumor transcriptomic data, it provided the initial clinical rationale to investigate a potential regulatory relationship between HIF1A and TARDBP . This hypothesis was subsequently validated through direct mechanistic experiments, as described below.

### Hypoxia induces TDP-43 expression through HIF1-dependent transcriptional regulation in CRC cells
Based on the positive clinical correlation observed between TARDBP and HIF1A , we hypothesized that TDP-43 expression is directly controlled by the master hypoxia regulator, HIF1, under hypoxic conditions. Under hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ), TARDBP mRNA and protein levels were significantly induced in a time-dependent manner in SW480 and HCT116 cells, paralleling the induction of HIF-1α protein ( Fig. 2 A, B). To investigate if this hypoxic induction is mediated by HIF1, we efficiently knocked down HIF1A using specific shRNAs ( Fig. 2 C, D). Notably, HIF1A depletion markedly attenuated the hypoxia-induced upregulation of TDP-43 protein ( Fig. 2 E), indicating that HIF1A is necessary for TDP-43 induction under hypoxia.

### The HIF1-TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells
After confirming the regulatory link between HIF-1α and TDP-43, we sought to evaluate the functional necessity of this axis in mediating hypoxia-driven cancer progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis. To functionally characterize the HIF1- TARDBP axis, we first established efficient TARDBP knockdown and HIF1A overexpression models in SW480 and HCT116 cells, as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting ( Fig. 3 A-D). Under hypoxic conditions, TARDBP depletion significantly attenuated hypoxia-induced cell proliferation, migration, and invasion ( Fig. 3 E-G). Crucially, these suppressive effects were markedly rescued by ectopic expression of HIF1A ( Fig. 3 E-G), indicating that HIF1 functions upstream of TDP-43 to drive these malignant behaviors.

### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.
While TDP-43 has been primarily studied in neurodegenerative diseases [ 17 , 18 ], emerging evidence underscores its role as a multifaceted RNA-binding protein that drives cancer progression through diverse post-transcriptional mechanisms. TDP-43 regulates gene expression by modulating alternative splicing, mRNA stability, miRNA biogenesis, and lncRNA interactions [ 10 ]. For example, in triple-negative breast

Notably, HIF1A depletion markedly attenuated the hypoxia-induced upregulation of TDP-43 protein ( Fig. 2 E), indicating that HIF1A is necessary for TDP-43 induction under hypoxia.

### The HIF1-TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells
After confirming the regulatory link between HIF-1α and TDP-43, we sought to evaluate the functional necessity of this axis in mediating hypoxia-driven cancer progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis. To functionally characterize the HIF1- TARDBP axis, we first established efficient TARDBP knockdown and HIF1A overexpression models in SW480 and HCT116 cells, as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting ( Fig. 3 A-D). Under hypoxic conditions, TARDBP depletion significantly attenuated hypoxia-induced cell proliferation, migration, and invasion ( Fig. 3 E-G). Crucially, these suppressive effects were markedly rescued by ectopic expression of HIF1A ( Fig. 3 E-G), indicating that HIF1 functions upstream of TDP-43 to drive these malignant behaviors.

### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.
While TDP-43 has been primarily studied in neurodegenerative diseases [ 17 , 18 ], emerging evidence underscores its role as a multifaceted RNA-binding protein that drives cancer progression through diverse post-transcriptional mechanisms. ### Highlights
• Hypoxia induces TDP-43 via HIF-1α binding to HRE3 in its promoter.
• TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA through RRM domain-mediated interaction.
• TARDBP knockdown suppresses CRC metastasis and angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo .
• TRIP6 rescues malignant phenotypes inhibited by TARDBP silencing.

### Graphical abstract
Under hypoxia, HIF1 binds to the HRE3 site and transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP . TDP-43, via its RRM1 and RRM2 domains, stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to enhance its expression, ultimately driving CRC cell migration, invasion, and angiogenesis.

### Introduction
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with tumor metastasis being the primary cause of treatment failure and poor prognosis [ 1 ]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in driving cancer progression, and hypoxia is a key hallmark of advanced solid tumors [ 2 ]. Rapidly proliferating cancer cells outstrip the oxygen supply from existing vasculature, creating hypoxic regions that activate adaptive signaling pathways [ 3 ]. Clinically, tumor hypoxia has been directly linked to more aggressive phenotypes and poor patient outcomes. For instance, studies using 18F-fluoromisonidazole (FMISO) PET imaging have demonstrated that significant hypoxia is a robust indicator of increased distant metastasis risk and higher rates of disease progression [ 4 , 5 ]. Furthermore, hypoxia has been identified as an independent predictor of poor overall survival (OS) in various clinical cohorts [ 6 ]. The master regulator of cellular response to hypoxia, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), orchestrates the expression of numerous genes promoting angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and invasion [ 7 ]. Notably, tumor angiogenesis, stimulated by hypoxia-induced factors like VEGF, is essential for supplying nutrients and oxygen, thereby facilitating tumor growth and metastatic spread. Despite the established role of hypoxia in CRC aggressiveness, the complete repertoire of downstream effectors and the intricate molecular networks linking hypoxia to CRC metastasis remain incompletely elucidated.
TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), encoded by the TARDBP gene, is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein predominantly known for its role in neurodegenerative diseases [ 8 , 9 ]. However, emerging evidence suggests an oncogenic function for TDP-43 in various cancers, where it regulates gene expression at multiple levels, including mRNA stability and alternative splicing [ 10 ]. TDP-43 contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM

### Bioinformatic analysis
The mRNA expression data of TARDBP (encoding TDP-43) and HIF1A in CRC and adjacent normal tissues were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ). The protein expression level of TDP-43 in colon cancer was analyzed using data from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) via the UALCAN portal ( http://ualcan.path.uab.edu ). The correlation between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in TCGA CRC samples was evaluated using Pearson’s correlation analysis.

### Animal housing
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Second Clinical College of Zhengzhou University and conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Female BALB/c nude mice (6 weeks old) were purchased from Beijing Huafukang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle, controlled temperature (22±2°C), and humidity (50±10%). Food and water were provided ad libitum. All efforts were made to minimize animal suffering.

### Results
TARDBP is upregulated in CRC and correlates with HIF1A expression
We first evaluated the clinical significance of TDP-43 in CRC by analyzing public datasets to determine whether its expression is altered in tumor tissues and associated with hypoxia-related signaling. Analysis of TCGA RNA-seq data revealed that TARDBP mRNA levels were significantly elevated in CRC tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues ( Fig. 1 A). Consistent with this finding, protein expression data from the CPTAC confirmed a significant increase in TDP-43 protein levels in colon tumors ( Fig. 1 B). Given the central role of hypoxia and its master regulator HIF-1α in cancer progression, we further examined their relationship. Notably, correlation analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in CRC cohorts (Pearson R =0.277, P &lt; 0.001) ( Fig. 1 C). While this relatively weak correlation likely reflects the cellular heterogeneity and temporal dynamics inherent to bulk tumor transcriptomic data, it provided the initial clinical rationale to investigate a potential regulatory relationship between HIF1A and TARDBP . This hypothesis was subsequently validated through direct mechanistic experiments, as described below.

### Hypoxia induces TDP-43 expression through HIF1-dependent transcriptional regulation in CRC cells
Based on the positive clinical correlation observed between TARDBP and HIF1A , we hypothesized that TDP-43 expression is directly controlled by the master hypoxia regulator, HIF1, under hypoxic conditions. Under hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ), TARDBP mRNA and protein levels were significantly induced in a time-dependent manner in SW480 and HCT116 cells, paralleling the induction of HIF-1α protein ( Fig. 2 A, B). To investigate if this hypoxic induction is mediated by HIF1, we efficiently knocked down HIF1A using specific shRNAs ( Fig. 2 C, D). Notably, HIF1A depletion markedly attenuated the hypoxia-induced upregulation of TDP-43 protein ( Fig. 2 E), indicating that HIF1A is necessary for TDP-43 induction under hypoxia.

### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.

### Highlights
• Hypoxia induces TDP-43 via HIF-1α binding to HRE3 in its promoter.
• TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA through RRM domain-mediated interaction.
• TARDBP knockdown suppresses CRC metastasis and angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo .
• TRIP6 rescues malignant phenotypes inhibited by TARDBP silencing.

### Graphical abstract
Under hypoxia, HIF1 binds to the HRE3 site and transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP . TDP-43, via its RRM1 and RRM2 domains, stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to enhance its expression, ultimately driving CRC cell migration, invasion, and angiogenesis.

### Introduction
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with tumor metastasis being the primary cause of treatment failure and poor prognosis [ 1 ]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in driving cancer progression, and hypoxia is a key hallmark of advanced solid tumors [ 2 ]. Rapidly proliferating cancer cells outstrip the oxygen supply from existing vasculature, creating hypoxic regions that activate adaptive signaling pathways [ 3 ]. Clinically, tumor hypoxia has been directly linked to more aggressive phenotypes and poor patient outcomes. For instance, studies using 18F-fluoromisonidazole (FMISO) PET imaging have demonstrated that significant hypoxia is a robust indicator of increased distant metastasis risk and higher rates of disease progression [ 4 , 5 ]. Furthermore, hypoxia has been identified as an independent predictor of poor overall survival (OS) in various clinical cohorts [ 6 ]. The master regulator of cellular response to hypoxia, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), orchestrates the expression of numerous genes promoting angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and invasion [ 7 ]. Notably, tumor angiogenesis, stimulated by hypoxia-induced factors like VEGF, is essential for supplying nutrients and oxygen, thereby facilitating tumor growth and metastatic spread. Despite the established role of hypoxia in CRC aggressiveness, the complete repertoire of downstream effectors and the intricate molecular networks linking hypoxia to CRC metastasis remain incompletely elucidated.
TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), encoded by the TARDBP gene, is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein predominantly known for its role in neurodegenerative diseases [ 8 , 9 ]. However, emerging evidence suggests an oncogenic function for TDP-43 in various cancers, where it regulates gene expression at multiple levels, including mRNA stability and alternative splicing [ 10 ]. TDP-43 contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM

### Bioinformatic analysis
The mRNA expression data of TARDBP (encoding TDP-43) and HIF1A in CRC and adjacent normal tissues were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ). The protein expression level of TDP-43 in colon cancer was analyzed using data from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) via the UALCAN portal ( http://ualcan.path.uab.edu ). The correlation between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in TCGA CRC samples was evaluated using Pearson’s correlation analysis.

### Animal housing
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Second Clinical College of Zhengzhou University and conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Female BALB/c nude mice (6 weeks old) were purchased from Beijing Huafukang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle, controlled temperature (22±2°C), and humidity (50±10%). Food and water were provided ad libitum. All efforts were made to minimize animal suffering.

### Results
TARDBP is upregulated in CRC and correlates with HIF1A expression
We first evaluated the clinical significance of TDP-43 in CRC by analyzing public datasets to determine whether its expression is altered in tumor tissues and associated with hypoxia-related signaling. Analysis of TCGA RNA-seq data revealed that TARDBP mRNA levels were significantly elevated in CRC tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues ( Fig. 1 A). Consistent with this finding, protein expression data from the CPTAC confirmed a significant increase in TDP-43 protein levels in colon tumors ( Fig. 1 B). Given the central role of hypoxia and its master regulator HIF-1α in cancer progression, we further examined their relationship. Notably, correlation analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in CRC cohorts (Pearson R =0.277, P &lt; 0.001) ( Fig. 1 C). While this relatively weak correlation likely reflects the cellular heterogeneity and temporal dynamics inherent to bulk tumor transcriptomic data, it provided the initial clinical rationale to investigate a potential regulatory relationship between HIF1A and TARDBP . This hypothesis was subsequently validated through direct mechanistic experiments, as described below.

### Hypoxia induces TDP-43 expression through HIF1-dependent transcriptional regulation in CRC cells
Based on the positive clinical correlation observed between TARDBP and HIF1A , we hypothesized that TDP-43 expression is directly controlled by the master hypoxia regulator, HIF1, under hypoxic conditions. Under hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ), TARDBP mRNA and protein levels were significantly induced in a time-dependent manner in SW480 and HCT116 cells, paralleling the induction of HIF-1α protein ( Fig. 2 A, B). To investigate if this hypoxic induction is mediated by HIF1, we efficiently knocked down HIF1A using specific shRNAs ( Fig. 2 C, D). Notably, HIF1A depletion markedly attenuated the hypoxia-induced upregulation of TDP-43 protein ( Fig. 2 E), indicating that HIF1A is necessary for TDP-43 induction under hypoxia.

(A-B) SW480 and HCT116 cells were exposed to hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ) for the indicated times. (A) TARDBP mRNA levels were measured by RT-qPCR. Data are normalized to normoxic control (0 h). (B) Protein levels of TDP-43 and HIF-1α were analyzed by Western blotting. β-actin served as a loading control. (C-D) Validation of HIF1A knockdown efficiency in SW480 and HCT116 cells transfected with shRNA targeting HIF1A (sh HIF1A ) or non-targeting control (shNC). Efficiency was confirmed by (C) RT-qPCR and (D) Western blotting. (E) Western blot analysis of TDP-43 protein levels in SW480 and HCT116 cells transfected with shNC or sh HIF1A and then exposed to hypoxia (1% O 2 , 24 h). (F) Luciferase reporter assay in HEK293T cells co-transfected with a TARDBP promoter reporter construct and either HIF1A overexpression plasmid ( HIF1A ) or empty vector control (Vec). Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity. (G) Luciferase activity of serial 5’-truncation mutants of the TARDBP promoter co-transfected with HIF1A into HEK293T cells. The location of putative hypoxia-response elements (HREs) is indicated. (H) ChIP assays w

### The HIF1-TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells
After confirming the regulatory link between HIF-1α and TDP-43, we sought to evaluate the functional necessity of this axis in mediating hypoxia-driven cancer progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis. To functionally characterize the HIF1- TARDBP axis, we first established efficient TARDBP knockdown and HIF1A overexpression models in SW480 and HCT116 cells, as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting ( Fig. 3 A-D). Under hypoxic conditions, TARDBP depletion significantly attenuated hypoxia-induced cell proliferation, migration, and invasion ( Fig. 3 E-G). Crucially, these suppressive effects were markedly rescued by ectopic expression of HIF1A ( Fig. 3 E-G), indicating that HIF1 functions upstream of TDP-43 to drive these malignant behaviors.
The HIF1- TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells. (A-D) Validation of gene manipulation efficiency. Knockdown and overexpression efficiency were confirmed by (A, C) qRT-PCR and (B, D) Western blotting. (E-I) Functional assays were performed in cells subjected to the following treatments: Normoxia, Hypoxia, Hypoxia+shNC, Hypoxia+sh TARDBP , Hypoxia+sh TARDBP +Vec, Hypoxia+sh TARDBP + HIF1A . (E) Cell proliferation was assessed by CCK-8 assay. (F) Cell migration was evaluated by Transwell assay (without Matrigel coating). Representative images (left) and quantitative analysis (right) are shown. (G) Cell invasion was evaluated by Transwell assay (with Matrigel coating). Representative images (left) and quantitative analysis (right) are shown. (H) Angiogenesis was assessed using the CAM assay. ### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.
While TDP-43 has been primarily studied in neurodegenerative diseases [ 17 , 18 ], emerging evidence underscores its role as a multifaceted RNA-binding protein that drives cancer progression through diverse post-transcriptional mechanisms. TDP-43 regulates gene expression by modulating alternative splicing, mRNA stability, miRNA biogenesis, and lncRNA interactions [ 10 ]. For example, in triple-negative breast

Transl Oncol . 2026 Jun 12;70:102817. doi: 10.1016/j.tranon.2026.102817
HIF1-driven TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to drive angiogenesis and colorectal cancer progression under hypoxia

### Highlights
• Hypoxia induces TDP-43 via HIF-1α binding to HRE3 in its promoter.
• TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA through RRM domain-mediated interaction.
• TARDBP knockdown suppresses CRC metastasis and angiogenesis in vitro and in vivo .
• TRIP6 rescues malignant phenotypes inhibited by TARDBP silencing.

### Graphical abstract
Under hypoxia, HIF1 binds to the HRE3 site and transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP . TDP-43, via its RRM1 and RRM2 domains, stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to enhance its expression, ultimately driving CRC cell migration, invasion, and angiogenesis.

### Introduction
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with tumor metastasis being the primary cause of treatment failure and poor prognosis [ 1 ]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) plays a critical role in driving cancer progression, and hypoxia is a key hallmark of advanced solid tumors [ 2 ]. Rapidly proliferating cancer cells outstrip the oxygen supply from existing vasculature, creating hypoxic regions that activate adaptive signaling pathways [ 3 ]. Clinically, tumor hypoxia has been directly linked to more aggressive phenotypes and poor patient outcomes. For instance, studies using 18F-fluoromisonidazole (FMISO) PET imaging have demonstrated that significant hypoxia is a robust indicator of increased distant metastasis risk and higher rates of disease progression [ 4 , 5 ]. Furthermore, hypoxia has been identified as an independent predictor of poor overall survival (OS) in various clinical cohorts [ 6 ]. The master regulator of cellular response to hypoxia, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), orchestrates the expression of numerous genes promoting angiogenesis, metabolic reprogramming, and invasion [ 7 ]. Notably, tumor angiogenesis, stimulated by hypoxia-induced factors like VEGF, is essential for supplying nutrients and oxygen, thereby facilitating tumor growth and metastatic spread. Despite the established role of hypoxia in CRC aggressiveness, the complete repertoire of downstream effectors and the intricate molecular networks linking hypoxia to CRC metastasis remain incompletely elucidated.
TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), encoded by the TARDBP gene, is a multifunctional RNA-binding protein predominantly known for its role in neurodegenerative diseases [ 8 , 9 ]. However, emerging evidence suggests an oncogenic function for TDP-43 in various cancers, where it regulates gene expression at multiple levels, including mRNA stability and alternative splicing [ 10 ]. TDP-43 contains two RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM

### Bioinformatic analysis
The mRNA expression data of TARDBP (encoding TDP-43) and HIF1A in CRC and adjacent normal tissues were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ ). The protein expression level of TDP-43 in colon cancer was analyzed using data from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) via the UALCAN portal ( http://ualcan.path.uab.edu ). The correlation between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in TCGA CRC samples was evaluated using Pearson’s correlation analysis.

### Animal housing
All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of the Second Clinical College of Zhengzhou University and conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Female BALB/c nude mice (6 weeks old) were purchased from Beijing Huafukang Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Mice were housed under specific pathogen-free (SPF) conditions with a 12 h light/dark cycle, controlled temperature (22±2°C), and humidity (50±10%). Food and water were provided ad libitum. All efforts were made to minimize animal suffering.

### Results
TARDBP is upregulated in CRC and correlates with HIF1A expression
We first evaluated the clinical significance of TDP-43 in CRC by analyzing public datasets to determine whether its expression is altered in tumor tissues and associated with hypoxia-related signaling. Analysis of TCGA RNA-seq data revealed that TARDBP mRNA levels were significantly elevated in CRC tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues ( Fig. 1 A). Consistent with this finding, protein expression data from the CPTAC confirmed a significant increase in TDP-43 protein levels in colon tumors ( Fig. 1 B). Given the central role of hypoxia and its master regulator HIF-1α in cancer progression, we further examined their relationship. Notably, correlation analysis demonstrated a significant positive association between TARDBP and HIF1A mRNA expression in CRC cohorts (Pearson R =0.277, P &lt; 0.001) ( Fig. 1 C). While this relatively weak correlation likely reflects the cellular heterogeneity and temporal dynamics inherent to bulk tumor transcriptomic data, it provided the initial clinical rationale to investigate a potential regulatory relationship between HIF1A and TARDBP . This hypothesis was subsequently validated through direct mechanistic experiments, as described below.

### Hypoxia induces TDP-43 expression through HIF1-dependent transcriptional regulation in CRC cells
Based on the positive clinical correlation observed between TARDBP and HIF1A , we hypothesized that TDP-43 expression is directly controlled by the master hypoxia regulator, HIF1, under hypoxic conditions. Under hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ), TARDBP mRNA and protein levels were significantly induced in a time-dependent manner in SW480 and HCT116 cells, paralleling the induction of HIF-1α protein ( Fig. 2 A, B). To investigate if this hypoxic induction is mediated by HIF1, we efficiently knocked down HIF1A using specific shRNAs ( Fig. 2 C, D). Notably, HIF1A depletion markedly attenuated the hypoxia-induced upregulation of TDP-43 protein ( Fig. 2 E), indicating that HIF1A is necessary for TDP-43 induction under hypoxia.

(A-B) SW480 and HCT116 cells were exposed to hypoxic conditions (1% O 2 ) for the indicated times. (A) TARDBP mRNA levels were measured by RT-qPCR. Data are normalized to normoxic control (0 h). (B) Protein levels of TDP-43 and HIF-1α were analyzed by Western blotting. β-actin served as a loading control. (C-D) Validation of HIF1A knockdown efficiency in SW480 and HCT116 cells transfected with shRNA targeting HIF1A (sh HIF1A ) or non-targeting control (shNC). Efficiency was confirmed by (C) RT-qPCR and (D) Western blotting. (E) Western blot analysis of TDP-43 protein levels in SW480 and HCT116 cells transfected with shNC or sh HIF1A and then exposed to hypoxia (1% O 2 , 24 h). (F) Luciferase reporter assay in HEK293T cells co-transfected with a TARDBP promoter reporter construct and either HIF1A overexpression plasmid ( HIF1A ) or empty vector control (Vec). Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity. (G) Luciferase activity of serial 5’-truncation mutants of the TARDBP promoter co-transfected with HIF1A into HEK293T cells. ### The HIF1-TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells
After confirming the regulatory link between HIF-1α and TDP-43, we sought to evaluate the functional necessity of this axis in mediating hypoxia-driven cancer progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis. To functionally characterize the HIF1- TARDBP axis, we first established efficient TARDBP knockdown and HIF1A overexpression models in SW480 and HCT116 cells, as confirmed by qRT-PCR and Western blotting ( Fig. 3 A-D). Under hypoxic conditions, TARDBP depletion significantly attenuated hypoxia-induced cell proliferation, migration, and invasion ( Fig. 3 E-G). Crucially, these suppressive effects were markedly rescued by ectopic expression of HIF1A ( Fig. 3 E-G), indicating that HIF1 functions upstream of TDP-43 to drive these malignant behaviors.
The HIF1- TARDBP axis promotes malignant phenotypes and VEGF secretion under hypoxia in CRC cells. (A-D) Validation of gene manipulation efficiency. SW480 and HCT116 cells were transfected with shRNA targeting TARDBP (sh TARDBP ) or non-targeting control (shNC) (A, B), or with a HIF1A overexpression plasmid ( HIF1A ) or empty vector control (Vec) (C, D). Knockdown and overexpression efficiency were confirmed by (A, C) qRT-PCR and (B, D) Western blotting. (E-I) Functional assays were performed in cells subjected to the following treatments: Normoxia, Hypoxia, Hypoxia+shNC, Hypoxia+sh TARDBP , Hypoxia+sh TARDBP +Vec, Hypoxia+sh TARDBP + HIF1A . (E) Cell proliferation was assessed by CCK-8 assay. (F) Cell migration was evaluated by Transwell assay (without Matrigel coating). Representative images (left) and quantitative analysis (right) are shown. (G) Cell invasion was evaluated by Transwell assay (with Matrigel coating). Representative images (left) and quantitative analysis (right) are shown. (H) Angiogenesis was assessed using the CAM assay. ### Discussion
CRC progression is strongly influenced by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment [ 15 ], yet the complete molecular mechanisms linking hypoxia to malignant phenotypes remain incompletely understood [ 15 , 16 ]. In this study, we systematically addressed our research objectives to elucidate these mechanisms, establishing a clear logical framework for our experimental design. First, we successfully identified the upstream regulation where HIF1 transcriptionally upregulates TARDBP through direct binding to a specific HRE3 in its promoter, fulfilling our first objective. Second, our functional assays provided robust evidence for the necessity of the HIF1/ TARDBP axis in driving malignant phenotypes, including proliferation, migration, invasion, and angiogenesis, both in vitro and in vivo , addressing our second objective. Finally, we characterized TRIP6 as the critical downstream mediator that fulfills our third objective. Together, these findings define a novel HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 signaling cascade that orchestrates the adaptive response of CRC cells to hypoxia.
The clinical significance of this axis is underscored by the direct correlation between hypoxia severity and tumor aggressiveness. Previous longitudinal imaging has shown that the onset and sustained presence of hypoxia strongly correlate with increased incidence of metastasis and unfavorable prognosis in cancer patients [ 4 , 6 ]. By establishing the HIF1/ TARDBP / TRIP6 cascade, we provide a concrete molecular link between the clinically observed hypoxic state and the aggressive metastatic behavior of CRC.
While TDP-43 has been primarily studied in neurodegenerative diseases [ 17 , 18 ], emerging evidence underscores its role as a multifaceted RNA-binding protein that drives cancer progression through diverse post-transcriptional mechanisms. TDP-43 regulates gene expression by modulating alternative splicing, mRNA stability, miRNA biogenesis, and lncRNA interactions [ 10 ]. For example, in triple-negative breast

Transl Oncol . 2026 Jun 12;70:102817. doi: 10.1016/j.tranon.2026.102817
HIF1-driven TDP-43 stabilizes TRIP6 mRNA to drive angiogenesis and colorectal cancer progression under hypoxia
